However, the advancement of AI through the use of vast amounts of data and extensive computational resources has led to a divergence in the objectives of the two fields. Failing to replicate the outcomes of AI when applied to biological systems does not imply that machines cannot outperform biological counterparts. Rather, it indicates a lack of understanding of the underlying mechanisms of both natural and artificial intelligence. To bridge this knowledge gap, a theoretical framework encompassing both fields is required. We propose a unified model of both fields, with a focus on both the inputs and internal workings of both systems. We suggest that a key component of both fields lies in the ability to represent the relationships between different aspects of both systems. We further suggest that a potential solution to the mystery of both fields could be found in graph-based neural networks. We discuss the implications of this hypothesis and outline several research questions that need to be addressed to validate this hypothesis.

Specifically, we consider the case where the free will of the agent can be defined in terms of a free will parameter.  We consider two specific free will definitions, namely the Markov property and the isomorphism property.  We show that both definitions can be redefined in terms of statistical properties, making it possible to estimate the free will parameter from observations of the agent's interactions with its environment.  Next, we present an alternative agent definition based on the splitting of states, making it possible to identify whether the agent distinguishes between environmental states that do not affect its future. of active galactic nuclei (AGN) has been extensively studied, yet the gravitational wave signal produced by an orbiting binary black hole (BBH) remains undetected.  A theoretical investigation is proposed to address this, by calculating light curves and spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and searching for the associated gravitational waves using Advanced LIGO/Virgo.  The study focuses on BBH systems that are accreting from a central torus and orbiting supermassive black holes in the mass range of 30 to 10^6 times the mass of the Sun, which are observable by current space and ground-based detectors.  The results show that these systems can produce significant optical and UV variability as well as gravitational wave signals, with the optical variability being most prominent for intermediate-mass BBH systems that are most likely to be detected.  The proposed model can also explain the observed rapid variability of some BBN systems, which has not been possible with other existing models.  The study provides a framework for jointly analyzing optical/UV variability and gravitational wave signals to constrain the properties of these systems and identify their transient electromagnetic counterparts.

However, the planning of a robust system is complicated by stochastic wind power demands and binary power flow constraints, which hinder mixed-integer linear programming-based approaches.  To overcome these challenges, we first apply Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions to derive first-order approximations of thermal constraints and second, use convex relaxations of the flow constraints to replace the approximations. We investigate the learning dynamics of the hard attention transformer (HAT) model during training with a mixture of hAT and full-attention (FULL) training approaches.  The hAT training approach trains the model to attend to all tokens at once,  whereas the FULL training approach trains the model to attend to a single token at a time.  The learning dynamics of the model are analyzed in terms of the model's attention distribution as it evolves during training.  Our analysis of the attention distribution under training reveals that training the model to focus on a single token (FULL training) results in an inhomogeneous attention distribution,  whereas training the model to give equal weight to all tokens (hAT training) leads to an increasingly homogeneous attention distribution.  Consequently, the model's performance is heavily influenced by the homogeneity of its attention distribution.  We also provide theoretical backing for the observed behavior of the attention distribution in a mean-field setting.

structure of polarized protons at high-buencies has been developed. It involves studying radiative deep-inelastic scattering off polarized protons in the leading-power approximation.  A formula was derived that expresses the twist-2 contribution to this process in terms of the polarized proton's distribution function. Unlike traditional methods, our approach avoids making quark-parton model assumptions. Instead, it employs light-cone correlation matrices involving a quark's light-cone position and its squared hadronic centre-of-mass frame time. As the average in-flight time becomes uncorrelated with the squared time, it signifies the onset of quark hadronization.

This paper presents a new weakly-supervised labeling method based on minimal user input and low-cost labels in the form of bounding boxes encompassing objects of interest. Our proposed approach aims to create a weak labeling scheme that minimizes the influence of irrelevant content within the bounding boxes on task performance. We introduce two innovative labeling methods: the Boundary Suppression Optimization Objective (BSOO) and the Boundary Suppressed Optimal Transport (BSOT). The BSOO framework generates precise labels by downweighting the impact of extra content in the bounding boxes, while the BSOT approach produces accurate labels through the generation of task-relevant masks, guided by the low-cost inclusive bounding boxes. We evaluate our methods on two prominent datasets, the MS-COCO and the ADE20K semantic segmentation benchmarks, and the results demonstrate the superiority of our weakly-supervised framework over existing approaches, particularly when utilizing the proposed BSOT labeling method.

In contrast, the storage of unlabeled images is relatively inexpensive and unbounded due to the ease of collecting them. Images can be used as pseudo-data, providing a cost-effective and flexible supplement to the limited particle data. In this study, we explore the potential of incorporating unlabeled images into deep learning algorithms for classifying particles, specifically using a particle data set and an images data set with distinct features. Initially, particles and images are treated separately, with models trained on each without knowledge of the other. Subsequently, we investigate two approaches to leverage the extensive images data in conjunction with the limited particle data. The first approach involves training a self-supervised model on the images, fine-tuning it on the particles, and then merging it with the model trained on the particles. The second approach involves training a self-supervised model on the images and adjusting it based on the particles. The results indicate that incorporating the images data leads to improved model performance compared to using only the particle data. The best outcome was achieved with the second approach, resulting in a 99.999999% accuracy rate for the 4-class classification task.

study of complex systems has seen substantial growth,  but a unified theory has yet to emerge.  Agents-based modeling has become a key area of focus within this discipline, but it has also become the subject of controversy.  We examine the controversy surrounding agents' rationality in economic models and explore how this debate reflects a broader issue concerning the rationality question in complex systems.  We analyze the strengths and weaknesses of two primary approaches to rationality in agents' behavior: prescriptive and descriptive.  Our investigation into complex systems reveals that the third route, where rationality is viewed as an emergent property resulting from the interplay between prescriptive and descriptive aspects, is more appropriate for complex systems.  Our paper proposes a new framework for understanding the rationality question in complex systems and offers a path forward for the controversy surrounding agents' rationality in agents-based modeling.

The long-standing issue of flavor in the supersymmetric model can be addressed within the Standard Model flavor framework. This study investigates the supersymmetric parameter space of extended scalar models, specifically focusing on the three-neutrino oscillation parameters, the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, and the absence of discovery in supersymmetry. We utilize the public code FLAVIA to calculate the flavor effects of these models and constrain their parameter space based on existing data. By combining this information with LHC constraints on the extended scalar sector and applying astrophysical constraints on self-interacting dark matter, we perform the first comprehensive analysis of a multi-dimensional supersymmetric parameter space within an extended scalar model. We consider models with additional Higgs bosons that interact with quarks, leptons, and dark matter, as well as models with additional Higgs triplets, and we derive stringent limits on the associated supersymmetric parameter. The results indicate that the supersymmetric parameter space is heavily constrained by direct searches for additional Higgs bosons and dark matter, as well as the need to explain the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, leaving only a few viable regions in models with dark matter interactions that are consistent with the long-lived particle searches.

Research has indicated that regular exercise can have a positive impact on individuals with MS, yet there has been limited investigation into high-intensity interval training (HIIT) specifically tailored for this group. In our study, we examined the effectiveness of an eight-week, 3-day per week, 40-minute a session HIIT program on physical and mental well-being in individuals with relapsing-remitting MS. Participants completed assessments of physical functioning, fatigue levels, and the Brief Fatigue Inventory (BFI) before and after completing the exercise program. Results showed significant improvements in physical functioning scores and reductions in fatigue levels following HIIT, with no adverse events reported. Our findings indicate that an 8-week HIIT regimen can enhance physical functioning and decrease fatigue in individuals with relapsing-remitting MS, and these high-intensity exercises were well-tolerated and completed without incident.

In this study, we extend this research to include a more complex scenario where the electron radiation is observed face-on, allowing for the derivation of "total" spectra that encompass both synchrotron and inverse Compton components. We employ a chi^2 minimization approach to reconstruct electron distributions from "total" spectra and investigate the feasibility of this method using model spectra representing particle-in-cell simulations. In contrast to previous results, we find that the chi^2 method can successfully recover simple power-law spectra down to a slope of Gamma = 3.5, but struggles with more complex distributions with significant photon components. Notably, we observe that synchrotron and inverse Compton spectra provide equally valuable information in this face-on configuration. We also investigate the impact of contamination from a pre-existing background and the difficulty of inverting quasi-power-law distributions. Our research highlights the importance of considering "total" spectra in contexts such as relativistic jets, where this approach can offer valuable insights.

a reliable communication system over a wireless channel with energy harvesting constraints is addressed. We examined a sample of z=2-3 spiral galaxies, utilizing a novel method that employs emission lines to measure their metallicity.  We found evidence of a distinct 'metallicity break' at z=1.5 in these galaxies, which seems to be a key factor in the history of spiral galaxies.  We discovered that below z=1.5, about 40% of the metallicity growth in these galaxies was due to star formation processes, which suddenly increased to 80% above that threshold.  We also found evidence of a similar break in above-average disk surface density galaxies, which occurred at z=2, which correlated with a similar increase in the fraction of star formation-derived gas.  We also discovered that above this threshold, above-average disk surface density galaxies were more efficient at converting gas into stars, which may have been caused by more intense star formation processes.  We also found that the cosmic star formation history has a significant impact on the distribution of gas in these galaxies, which may have contributed to the 'metallicity break' we observed.  We also discovered that a significant amount of gas in these galaxies above z=1.5 comes from above their virial radii, which may have been caused by above-average gas accretion rates in these galaxies.

This paper takes a different approach, theoretically analyzing a neural network-based model known as the wave equation-based neural network (WENN). Specifically, the WENN minimizes a regularization term for a source inverse problem by employing a time-domain neural network to estimate the source function. We establish the well-posedness of the optimization problem we consider and demonstrate the uniqueness of solutions under certain conditions. Furthermore, we prove that the WENN has the capability to solve a broad class of source inverse problems directly, even those involving non-uniqueness. This direct solution property of the WENN has not been shown for most types of neural network-based models. We provide theoretical justification for the WENN's direct solution capability by analyzing its associated stationary problem and showing equivalence to a standard inverse problem solution under certain conditions. This study could offer new insights for solving a wide range of inverse problems using neural network-based approaches.

background noise in gravitational wave detectors stems from scattered thermal radiation.  In order to minimize this effect, detectors like LIGO employ wavelength plate pairs to cancel out scattered light.  However, conventional materials for these plates are insufficient due to their limited wavelength sensitivity.  We propose a novel approach utilizing photonic crystals as the plates, which exhibit a significantly broader operational wavelength range.  By incorporating such plates, we demonstrate the ability to precisely measure extremely minute strain changes.  Specifically, our calculations show that a 20-meter long setup with our proposed plates can achieve a remarkable sensitivity of $10^{-24} m/m$ at $1 kHz$ frequency.  This level of sensitivity could enable the detection of gravitational wave events previously obscured by the limit set by scattered thermal radiation.

This paper investigates the fault tolerance of blockchain consensus protocols based on proof of work, specifically focusing on scenarios where the majority of network participants can act maliciously.  Initially, the research examines a broad class of blockchain consensus protocols that incorporate a secondary channel for verifying newly added blocks.  The researchers developed and demonstrated a test to determine whether certain malicious operators can manipulate the order in which blocks are issued on the main chain.  If the test is passed, it implies that there is only one valid blockchain at any given time, the longest chain property holds, and the network can maintain a steady block issuance rate.  If the test is failed, it opens up the possibility of creating short-chain attacks, such as the gray-median attack.  The paper also presents a test that can be used to evaluate the security of various blockchain protocols and provides results on the susceptibility of several existing protocols to manipulation.

We investigate the role of price within a broader framework that encompasses elements such as trust, cooperation, and reputation.  We develop a theoretical model where price emerges as a mechanism that reflects collective values, and we explore its impact on overall welfare.  We analyze how adopting strategies that prioritize welfare enhances overall wealth, and we verify this hypothesis through a series of experiments involving over 1,000 participants. the interstellar medium significantly impacts the propagation of cosmic rays and influences star formation through its influence on gaseous dynamics.  The ORION collaboration has developed a sophisticated three-dimensional simulation that incorporates large scale magnetic fields into the MHD gas dynamics within a galaxy.  The simulation utilizes adaptive mesh refinement and high order schemes to accurately model the complex interactions of magnetic fields and gaseous matter.  By analyzing the effects of magnetic fields on star formation, we have discovered that they can create highly localized regions of intense magnetism that interact with gas to form dense filaments and molecular clouds.  These structures are characterized by their alignment with magnetic fields and can give rise to massive density contrasts, potentially leading to the formation of prestellar cores and providing an explanation for observed far-infrared observations.  The collaboration's work has also identified distinct patterns of far-ultraviolet and infrared emission that are consistent with observed data from the Milky Way and other galaxies.

Social media platforms, with their vast amount of data, can be a valuable resource, but the unstructured nature of the information poses a challenge. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing the need for labeled data and computational resources, which has significant implications for sentiment analysis applications in resource-constrained environments.

A key aspect of these variations lies in their affinity for a particular target, which is crucial for their functionality. In this context, we investigate a scenario in which an $SU(Nc)$ dark sector, featuring dark baryon parity symmetry, spontaneously breaks, leading to mass generation for both the EW and the dark sector.  The dark sector contains a first order phase transition due to the $SU(Nc)$ dynamics, which can be driven by the Higgs portal.  The symmetry breaking of the $SU(Nc)$ dark sector generates composite dark baryons as ADM, with the resulting relic density being a function of the $SU(Nc)$ temperature and its associated parameters.  The phase transition in the $SU(Nc)$ dark sector can be precisely modeled using lattice techniques, enabling the calculation of relevant parameters such as the latent heat and friction, which in turn can be used to constrain the resulting gravitational wave (GW) spectrum.  The constraints from the GW spectrum can be further influenced by the phase transition in the Higgs sector, which generates additional entropy and dilutes the ADM.  The resulting GW spectrum is constrained by LISA, PPTA, and pulsar timing arrays, with the constraints varying depending on the specific parameters of the model. Dengue fever is a significant public health issue caused by the dengue virus, which is spread by Aedes mosquitoes. The incubation period for dengue fever is 5-14 days, and symptoms can range from mild to severe, with some individuals remaining asymptomatic. Severe dengue fever may lead to complications such as bleeding, organ failure, and shock, and can be fatal. Dengue fever diagnosis is typically made through blood tests, and treatment is mainly supportive, with no specific antiviral therapy available. The development of the Dengue Fever Detection System (DDSys) is a response to the need for a more efficient and user-friendly method of diagnosing dengue fever. DDSys is a web-based platform that combines skin symptom analysis and patient information to assist medical professionals in diagnosing and managing dengue fever cases.

A Cameron-Liebler $k$-scheme of rank $r$ comprises a collection $\mathcal A$ of subspaces in $\Gamma(n,q)$ with the property that for any basis element $f$ of $V_n$, the number of subspaces in $\mathcal A$ containing a fixed vector is consistently proportional to $r$. We begin by exploring the fundamental parameters associated with these schemes and then derive several results related to the CL-rank of specific configurations. In particular, we demonstrate that every Cameron-Liebler $k$-scheme must have an rank $r$ that is odd, and also provide in the process, a fresh proof of a well-established identity in combinatorics concerning the expansion coefficients of a polynomial. Furthermore, we investigate necessary conditions for the existence of Cameron-Liebler $r$-schemes where $r \leq k$. Our analysis yields a notable application, confirming that no such schemes exist for any of the $r$-schemes of the vector space $V_n(q)$ when the space subspaces are planes over the binary field and the scheme rank equals the plane dimension.

in astrophysical and geophysical fluids, researchers rely on the quasi-linear approximation to derive closed equations for turbulent fluxes, specifically Reynolds and Hall-Shear fluxes, which drive large-scale mean flow changes.  However, this approximation's accuracy is questionable, especially when assessing Reynolds and shear stress predictions.  Our study employs direct numerical simulations of sheared Rayleigh-Benard convection and evaluates the quasi-linear approximation's validity by comparing predicted Reynolds and shear fluxes to those obtained from simulations.  The discrepancy between predicted and actual fluxes is substantial, exceeding the flux itself in certain cases.  Nevertheless, the approximation appears to be reasonably accurate, overestimating shear fluxes by a factor of 10 less than the flux in certain scenarios.  The mean flux partitioning is also influenced by the Prandtl number, with the shear flux dominating at low Prandtl numbers and being surpassed by the Reynolds flux at higher Prandtl numbers.

Our work is centered on a text-based dialogue dataset that incorporates multi-turn, multi-rank interactions across diverse topics.  Text2Speech dialogue data, which features spoken language interactions, presents a unique challenge due to its complex structure.  Existing continual learning approaches for task-oriented dialogue have been limited by one-turn, single-rank datasets and have not been able to address the challenges posed by natural language conversations.  To overcome this obstacle, we have developed a novel framework for task-oriented dialogue that encompasses four key components: a sentence embedding-based model for ranking responses, a sentence embedding-based model for generating the next turn in a conversation, a method for evaluating the quality of dialogue, and a novel cross-quality loss function that links these two models. We investigate this question by considering two unentangled qubits interacting with a common bath of bosons and find the answer depends heavily on the qubits' location relative to each other.  When the qubits are close together, their entanglement builds up at a rate that can be made arbitrarily small, but as their separation increases, a minimum distance emerges beyond which the entanglement generation rate becomes constant. This research specifically focuses on two existing variations of metric spaces: b-metric spaces and G-metric spaces. The new concept of b-G-convergence and the b-G-Cauchy sequence, along with the b-G-compactness, exhibit distinct characteristics. ann-Hilbert problem for second order linear ordinary differential equations can have transcendent solutions, yet most solutions to this problem possess finite integrals. Our study presents solutions to the Riemann-Hilbert problem for ordinary differential equations with three independent variables and three powers. The Fuchsian equation associated with this problem conformally maps to a hyperelastic differential equation after solving the Riemann-Hilbert problem. Consequently, nearly all solutions to this problem are elasto-plastic in nature. The integration of this hyperelastic equation yields an expression of the form dW/dz = sqrt(elastic polynomial). Our analysis focuses specifically on solutions where the elastic polynomial is of the third degree. Under certain conditions, these solutions can be expressed as nearly all W(z) = z_0 + integral from z_0 to z of the cubic root of (t-a)(t-b) dt. The associated solutions to the Riemann-Hilbert problem display three branch points and exhibit periodicity across two distinct periods, with monodromy matrices taking the form of translations.

This work explores the concept of generalized squeezed states within a specific quantum model, known as the Rabi model, which examines the interaction between a single two-level system and a specific quantum field. This particular model serves as a fundamental building block in various fields, including cavity electrodynamics, quantum optics, and cavity quantum electrodynamics. A set of states has been developed that encompasses several types of quantum state families, including those with reduced uncertainty, states with quantum entanglement, and state quasi-absence. This new set of states can be considered a set of generalized squeezed states in a specific Rabi model, and it has been established that this model's parameters can be adjusted to create states with better performance than standard quantum state theories. Furthermore, a state has been created in this model that cannot be created through the process of quantum entanglement. State quasi-absence has also been found in this model, and it has been demonstrated that this state can be created in a specific Rabi model with certain characteristics. This new model's states are considered a set of generalized squeezed states, and this study has significant implications for quantum information processing, such as the development of Rabi qubits, and can be used to create states with better performance than standard quantum state theories.

However, traditional approaches often compromise initial knowledge when learning new concepts due to the inherent nature of neural network optimization. This issue gives rise to catastrophic interference, an unwanted phenomenon that diminishes initial knowledge. In this investigation, we explore another adverse effect, namely backward interference, where new training disrupts old performance. We delve into its origins, characteristics, and consequences, and propose an innovative adaptation algorithm, called backward interference minimization (BIM), to mitigate this phenomenon. BIM leverages old tasks to constrain new training, effectively preventing backward interference. We evaluate our method across multiple datasets and network architectures, demonstrating its superior accuracy compared to conventional continual learning techniques. Moreover, our approach exhibits remarkable robustness, outperforming baseline methods in average accuracy by a significant margin of up to 10%.

This mechanism is expected to be a key factor in $J/\psi$ suppression observed in heavy ion collisions at higher energies.  However, recent findings from RHIC and the LHC suggest that $J/\psi$ is already suppressed in A+A collisions at low energies and small systems, well before the critical condition of the medium is met. One of the key approaches to this problem involves the development of high-performing machine learning models that can classify text as either offensive or non-offensive. To address this issue, researchers have developed post-hoc models called surrogates that predict labels based on the original network's output.  These surrogates have been evaluated using standard metrics like accuracy and F1-score, but they fail to consider the trade-off between performance and interpretability.  In this research, we introduce a novel evaluation framework that quantifies the trade-off between a surrogate's performance and its interpretability.  Our proposed method involves two key components: an intrinsic interpretability metric that measures the structural similarity between the original network and the surrogate, and an extrinsic interpretability metric that assesses the complexity of the surrogate.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our evaluation framework through both synthetic and real-world datasets, and our findings highlight the challenges in creating an optimal linear relationship between performance and interpretability.  Our framework provides a valuable tool for researchers to design and assess neural surrogate models that balance performance and interpretability.

This shortcoming could be addressed by incorporating visual cues that provide information about nearby people's health status, a concept that could potentially lead to a more effective approach to designing apps for active prevention.  Building on this idea, we present a prototype called $PreTrace$, a system that utilizes a smartphone and an external sensing device to facilitate the sharing of proximity information among users.  $PreTrace$ employs auditory feedback to inform users about the potential health risks associated with people in close proximity, a feature that draws inspiration from existing visual cue technologies and adapts them for an interactive mobile experience. in wide-bandgap semiconductors and dielectrics is a critical process that significantly influences their optical properties.  The exciton binding energy, which is an indicator of exciton stability, can be calculated using a simple two-band model, primarily applicable to semiconductors with low symmetry.  However, in wide-bandgap materials with low symmetry, additional complex band contributions hinder analytical solutions.  This study presents a method to address this challenge by deriving explicit expressions for both exciton and hole kinetic energies based on effective mass theory.  These formulas take into account the influence of kinetic energy spreading over the exciton wavefunction.  Our approach yields a comprehensive understanding of exciton behavior in a wide range of semiconductor materials, including zinc blende and wurtzite semiconductors and alloys, as well as polar and nonpolar dielectrics.

The observed features in the specific heat, including an electronic $\gamma T$ term, an elastic $\beta T^2$ term, and a peak associated with the superconducting phase, are analyzed. Bose-Einstein condensate in a one-dimensional optical lattice, subject to site-to-site disorder, as it relaxes from a sudden expansion. In the metallic phase, a universal power law governs the growth of domain sizes and mass currents, with an exponent that varies in response to lattice parameters.  In contrast, the insulating phase exhibits an exponential decay of domain sizes and currents, alongside a characteristic length scale that grows according to a power law with a variable exponent.   protocols, particularly in the context of protocols that use communication
  patterns with limited information sharing.  It's well established that any
  protocol for achieving consensus among n processes requires at least Omega(log
  n) bits of communication per message, on average.  However, this lower bound is
  based on the total amount of communication, rather than considering the
  complexities of different input distributions.  In this paper, we establish a new
  lower bound for protocols that use communication patterns with limited
  information sharing.  Specifically, we demonstrate that for any distribution D,
  there's a consensus protocol with communication sharing that has a
  (D, n)-message complexity equal to the product of the protocol's
  (D,n)-round complexity and its bit complexity.  Moreover, there exists a
  protocol that uses an O(log n)-round, process decision tree depth of 1, and
  achieves consensus with a process decision tree depth of 1.  This new lower
  bound has several implications for the design of efficient consensus protocols.

accretion disks can generate relativistic jets through various mechanisms. This paper investigates the BZ process in a Kerr black hole surrounded by a slim disk, taking into account magnetic interactions between the disk and hole as well as the general conservation of angular momentum.  A new model is proposed that considers the effects of a magnetized slim disk on the BZ process, and this model is applied to the relativistic outflow from NGC 1275.  This application demonstrates that the BZ process can contribute significantly to the observed jet power in this active galactic nucleus. within an Einstein-Maxwell-Schrodinger framework, we investigate how a background photon field influences the formation of black holes in binary neutron star mergers. We discover that the photon field substantially amplifies the oscillations of the neutron stars, leading to significant energy and momentum transfer between them. As the photon field intensifies, it causes more rapid accretion by the recollapsing hyper-massive neutron star, thereby enhancing its sensitivity to the composition of the particle-particle-photon mixture. We also observe that the background photon field can completely inhibit black hole formation, allowing the formation of long-lived, stable Schrodinger stars with masses up to approximately 2.7 times the solar mass. The presence of the photon field can extend the period of gravitational wave signals from binary neutron star mergers, with Schrodinger stars potentially emitting such waves for more than 10 seconds after the merger. These results indicate that binary neutron star mergers in the presence of strong photon fields can place more stringent constraints on axion-photon coupling than current laboratory experiments.

when students learn about recursion, specifically in relation to other key programming concepts like iteration.  Research has indicated that introducing recursion before iteration can actually hinder students' overall understanding of the topic.  To investigate this issue further, our study explores how introducing recursion before iteration affects students' ability to grasp program behavior.  In a series of experiments, we found that students who learn about recursion before iteration have a more difficult time creating programs that accurately model simple iterative processes.  However, this difficulty is not present when they are asked to design iterative programs that do not involve recursion.  Our research also indicates that iteration plays a crucial role in developing an intuitive understanding of iterative processes.  As a result, we propose that iteration should be taught before recursion in programming education.

of an electron in a strong laser field within a metal, employing a tight-binding Hamiltonian in the presence of circularly polarized light. In this study, we assess the robustness of pre-trained language models against Turing-normalized (TN) adversarial perturbations, a class of model-agnostic updates that maintain human intelligibility.  We begin by formulating a general framework for evaluating and guiding the development of TN-adversarial updates, a challenging task due to its non-differentiable and combinatorial nature.  Leveraging this framework, we experimentally evaluate several classes of updates on multiple models and datasets, finding that the framework can be effectively used to enhance model robustness, a difficult achievement given the trade-off between intelligibility and accuracy.  In our assessments, we found that the BERT-base model's predictions remain relatively stable (around 60% robust accuracy) under 10% TN updates, a metric that serves as a proxy for human judgment of slightly altered texts.  In contrast, we found that naive optimization methods resulted in updates that models could tolerate but were significantly altered (over 90% Hamming distance), a level of change that would be unlikely to be accepted by humans.

Perot cavity is used to create a selective feedback system for a laser that generates single photons through four-wave mixing in a $\chi^{(2)}$ crystal.  By placing the cavity after the non-linear crystal, only photons resonating within the cavity are fed back into the system.  This forces a preference for resonating photons, enhancing the generation of entangled photon pairs through resonant down-conversion.  As a result, the generation of photons that do not form pairs is significantly reduced.  The feedback mechanism is capable of increasing the pair entanglement while reducing the generation of non-paired photons to around 10% of the paired photons.  The feedback mechanism is also capable of controlling the degree of entanglement, which can be utilized to mitigate the impact of residual non-paired photons on a quantum information processing system.

AMV) is a decadal-scale climate pattern that can influence the frequency of El Ni\u00f1o events and affect global climate. Researchers are investigating the mechanisms driving AMV, which may involve natural feedback loops in the ocean and atmosphere or be a result of anthropogenic climate change. In this study, we utilize a comprehensive Earth system model to simulate AMV and identify its underlying causes. We find that the model exhibits multiple climate patterns that interact to create AMV, which we break down into two components: one caused by natural processes and another by human-induced processes. The natural component is primarily driven by a coupling between the ocean and atmosphere, which is initiated by the impact of human-induced warming on the atmosphere. This interaction is further complicated by the influence of clouds and the heat they trap. The human-induced component is caused by the interaction between the ocean and atmosphere, which is initiated by the direct impact of human-induced warming on the ocean. This interaction is also influenced by the impact of human-induced changes in the atmosphere on the ocean. Overall, this study provides a detailed understanding of the complex processes driving AMV, which can inform future research and climate change mitigation efforts.

Customers arrive according to an arbitrary distribution, and both sojourn times of customers in the system and the times between customer arrivals are modeled by general discrete phase-type distributions.  Each customer consists of $k$ independent phases, with $k$ being an arbitrary positive integer.  Furthermore, each server has a distinct set of states and transitions governed by its own discrete, state-dependent semi-Markov process.  Customers are served in a last-come, first-served order, with all customers waiting in a single infinite queue.  The number of customers waiting is described by an arbitrary discrete distribution.  Each server's service time corresponds to the time from when a customer enters the system until one of their phases is completed.  The paper derives the steady-state probabilities for the discrete phase-type times between customer arrivals and the resulting system lifetime expressed in closed form.  The paper also presents the mean lifetime of the system in closed form and calculates the mean lifetime for the specific case of a single-customer queue.

One challenge in this task is that text can be rotated in any direction, which makes it difficult to address using traditional text detection methods.  To overcome this limitation, researchers have started to explore the possibility of treating this task as a free-form image dewarping problem, which involves restoring the original content of the text by mapping it onto a planar surface.  This paper proposes a novel text detection framework, which combines a region-based proposal generation network and a region-based attention-guided transformer that refines the proposals and recovers the text content.  To ensure accurate restoration of the text, a multi-scale attention mechanism is introduced to preserve the structure of the text.  To address data scarcity, a pseudo-label generation method is also presented to automatically generate training data from unlabeled images.  To further improve performance on real-world datasets, a knowledge distillation method is proposed to learn from high-performing CNN models.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in detecting and recognizing 3D scene text.

By leveraging matrix calculus, we derive analytical expressions for the derivatives of image transformation functions, which can significantly accelerate computational processes. Although this method has been known for several decades, it remains underutilized in medical image registration algorithms. Although some researchers have applied this method to optimization problems in image transformation, the problems differ from those in medical image registration. In this study, we develop an efficient optimization algorithm for medical image registration based on this derivative calculation method. Although this algorithm demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods in experimental tests, it achieves similar results with fewer computational steps. Although this method shows significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods in terms of efficiency, it can be applied to a broader range of medical imaging tasks beyond image registration. By utilizing this derivative calculation method, we can enhance the speed and accuracy of image analysis tools, ultimately benefiting medical professionals in diagnosing and treating patients.

    evaluation of the quality of the generated output is a key challenge.  The
    evaluation of the translation quality is typically done by comparing the
    generated output to a reference output, and evaluation metrics are used to
    quantify the similarity between the two.  Traditional evaluation metrics,
    such as BLEU, rely on n-gram matching between the generated output and the
    reference output, but these metrics have limitations in capturing the
    overall meaning of the generated output.  In contrast, semantic evaluation
    metrics, such as BERTScore and BERT, use pre-trained language models to
    encode the generated output and the reference output into semantic vectors,
    and then compare the similarity between the two.  This paper provides an
    in-depth analysis of BERTScore, BERT, and other semantic evaluation metrics,
    and demonstrates their effectiveness in evaluating machine translation
    quality.  Our experiments show that BERTScore and BERT outperform traditional
    evaluation metrics in capturing the overall meaning of the generated output,
    and we discuss the advantages and challenges of using these metrics.

erial Vehicles (UAVs) is expanding rapidly, presenting new challenges for maintaining secure communications between UAVs and ground users.  The concept of using a trusted relay to facilitate this communication has been thoroughly examined in previous studies.  The current study investigates a new scenario in which the characteristics of an uncooperative relay are unknown, and both its position and transmission content are unclear.  The proposed cooperative security scheme employs a pair of uncooperative relays to communicate with a legitimate user through an active attack relay that can either amplify-and-forward (AF) or decode-and-forward (DF) signals.  The system's performance is evaluated under both relay protocols, considering the impact of different uncooperative relay behaviors.  The study derives closed-form expressions for outage probability and ergodic capacity, considering the behavior of the uncooperative relays.  Monte Carlo simulations are used to validate the theoretical results and explore the system's ergodic capacity.  The study reveals that employing DF scheme results in higher ergodic capacity than AF scheme, and increasing the number of uncooperative relays can improve system security.  The study also finds that the proposed cooperative security scheme outperforms a baseline scheme in terms of ergodic capacity.

gamma,p$)$^{22}$Ne reaction at 18.5 MeV has been studied experimentally, with a proton angular distribution measured from 5 to 25 degrees.  Three resonances at energies 17.85 MeV, 20.05 MeV, and 22.05 MeV have been identified with spins and parities $1/2^-$, $1/2^-$ and $5/2^-$ respectively.  Na2Ne compound nuclear formation cross sections have been derived and a reaction code TALYS-1.9.6 has been used to calculate cross sections for comparison with experimental data.  The sodium-23 gamma neutron capture cross sections for resonances have been estimated and a neutron capture experiment on $^{22}$Ne has been used to validate the results.  The $1/2^-$ resonance at 17.85 MeV has a width of 140 keV, with both radiative and neutron channels contributing equally.  The $1/2^-$ resonance at 20.05 MeV has a width of 190 keV, with the radiative channel being more prominent.  The $5/2^-$ resonance at 22.05 MeV has a width of 400 keV, with both radiative and neutron channels contributing equally.

This process typically results in axions being created with a spectrum that is too broad to match the required density of dark matter.  However, if the initial conditions for a second phase of inflation are sufficiently chaotic, it can limit the number of ULA particles created during the first phase by acting as a collapse trigger. spin state in graphene nanoribbons is a key area of research.  The proposed structure known as the spin quantum dot/interferometer consists of a spin quantum dot and a spin quantum path made of a zigzag graphene nanoribbon.  A method is presented to control the transverse spin state using a magnetic field and an inter-edge potential.  Our findings show that the spin Zeeman effect and the transverse spin resonance phenomenon can be utilized to filter out specific sub-bands and achieve unitary transverse spin polarization.  The interplay between the spin Zeeman effect and the quantum interference effect provides a means to control the transverse spin polarization.  The spin quantum dot/interferometer structure is demonstrated as an ideal design for developing spin quantum devices with functionalities such as spin filters and polarization-dependent spin quantum switches.

MRI, researchers can now track heart motion by analyzing multiple time points, thus providing morphological and motion information in MRI images.  This feature is highly desirable for correcting intensity issues in single-time point MRI images.  Unfortunately, existing motion estimation methods rely on conventional approaches that are computationally expensive and do not consider the constraints of physical motion.  This research presents a Cardiac Flow-Constrained Convolutional Network (CFCNet), an end-to-end Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model that refines motion estimation in Cine MRI images.  By integrating a novel Flow-Constrained module into the network, CFCNet ensures that motion constraints are met during the prediction process.  This constraint significantly reduces unnecessary computations and refines predictions, resulting in an improvement in accuracy of approximately 10% compared to a baseline model.  Furthermore, by reducing the output channels by half, computational costs are significantly reduced, making the model more efficient.  This research demonstrates that incorporating physical constraints into deep learning frameworks can enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of medical image analysis tasks.

scalar field behavior in a Kerr-Newman black hole environment is investigated. We analyze the impact of spin on the occurrence of the mass inflation phenomenon and the final state of the collapsing object, both of which are influenced by the object's spin. Results indicate that the mass inflation phenomenon occurs regardless of the massive scalar field's spin, but the final state of the collapsing object is highly dependent on the spin. When the spin exceeds a certain threshold, the mass of the resulting remnant decreases as the spin increases, mirroring the behavior observed in Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory. 1054 AD was extensively observed, the associated remnant is not fully understood.  Observations reveal a complex structure within the Crab Nebula, consisting of multiple coexisting scales and domains, each characterized by its own physical processes.  Therefore, describing the overall structure of the remnant as a singular system is oversimplified.  Instead, we propose viewing it as a collection of interlinked components, where interactions between them shape the overall structure.  We specifically focus on two components: the central pulsar wind nebula and the outer shock regions, which may not be directly connected.  We identify several key challenges hindering our understanding of the Crab remnant, including its energy balance, mass balance, and magnetic field configuration.  Existing models attempting to reconcile these features often struggle to account for all aspects of the remnant's structure.  We suggest viewing these discrepancies as indications of distinct domains that require separate consideration.  We discuss the advantages of adopting a multi-scale approach to studying planetary nebulae, which involves analyzing each domain on its own terms and examining the interaction between components that may not be consistent with global constraints.  This perspective offers a more nuanced understanding of planetary nebulae and may provide new insights into their complex structures.

Q-balls composed of multiple Q-charges exist within a given theory, offer the potential to explain multiple Baryon and Lepton number asymmetries in early Universe. a two-dimensional
  lattice model of interacting electrons in the presence of a strong magnetic field. The model exhibits the quantum Hall effect at high filling factors, exhibiting classical Drude conductivity in these regions. In contrast, the model predicts a vanishing conductivity for both charge and heat at the edge of these plateaus, which is attributed to the conservation of both energy and particle number. This behavior differs from other models, which forecast quantized thermal conductivity in the vicinity of half-integer plateaus. Our model, however, does not support any steady-state heat flow between reservoirs at different temperatures. This is because any such heat flow would need to be accompanied by a corresponding particle flow, which would also need to be completely dissipated in order to reach a steady state. As a result, the thermal conductivity of the model is independent of the temperature of the reservoirs which implies that the concept of thermal conductivity may not be applicable to systems exhibiting the quantum Hall effect.

By examining the thermodynamics of heat engines operating on a closed loop, we can gain valuable insights into how a driven quantum system responds to control parameters.  Although a wide range of models of driven quantum systems have been studied extensively, their non-equilibrium properties remain largely unexplored. Dense summarization produces a continuous time segment that covers the majority of the video content, whereas sparse summarization generates non-contiguous key events as output. Existing research has primarily focused on one type of summarization at a time. This paper introduces a unified framework that handles both summarization types simultaneously. This generalization allows for a more comprehensive representation of non-projective measurements, including those that exhibit increased sensitivity to measurement location. Building upon this development, our model utilizes spin measurements on a moving qubit to demonstrate the impact of context on average measurement outcomes and entanglement generation. Specifically, our findings show that moving qubits can yield counterintuitive results, such as obtaining average outcomes outside the expected range and entanglement generation from initially separable states. These effects are further amplified by spin measurements that are more sensitive to context, and can also be observed in stationary measurements. We derived the behavior of particles and fields in such a model and determined the periodicity of the extra dimensions. This periodicity can, however, be expressed as the ratio of two periods with a specific length scale.   increasingly complex challenge.  Our research proposes a novel protocol,
  called MultiNTP, to effectively synchronize time across devices that
  may be compromised.  The protocol leverages a Byzantine consensus
  mechanism to ensure that a majority of trustworthy collectors agree on
  a time offset relative to server time.  The protocol allows for a
  synchronization accuracy that scales inversely with the square of the
  time offset, and is feasible even when the majority of collectors are

  concept implementation of MultiNTP is available in the public domain,
  and our evaluation using this implementation demonstrates the efficacy
  of our approach.  Specifically, with collectors experiencing
  Byzantine faults, MultiNTP achieves an average synchronization
  accuracy of 100 milliseconds with a maximum latency of 150 milliseconds
  and a range of 250 milliseconds.  In contrast, the standard NTP
  protocol fails to achieve comparable results under the same conditions,
  resulting in an average accuracy of 1.1 seconds, a latency of 2.1

AOMs) are widely used in various optical systems, including those that detect gravitational waves.  As AOMs operate at high frequencies, they generate significant amounts of acousto-optic noise.  This study investigates the characteristics of AOM noise by modeling its random behavior as it affects the amplitude and frequency of light.  By applying this model to an interferometer and conducting actual measurements using Advanced LIGO detectors, we discovered that AOM noise exhibits distinct time and amplitude variations.  It is found to follow an approximate $1/f^{\alpha}$ pattern with $\alpha$ ranging from 0.2 to 0.5, and its energy levels differ between the detectors and vary across different frequency bands.  At higher frequencies beyond 100 Hz, the noise typically has an $\alpha$ value of approximately 0.2 and matches the observed noise in the detectors.  However, lower frequency aom noise exhibits higher energy levels and may pose challenges for detectors in the future.  To mitigate these effects, we propose several potential solutions.

ients (FXRTs) are highly luminous X-ray sources,  located outside the Milky Way, that suddenly appear and disappear in fast X-rays.  These enigmatic objects are thought to be associated with extreme events,  such as the sudden destruction of stars falling into supermassive black holes or the merging of compact objects.  Despite their significance, few of these FXRTs have been confirmed due to the scarcity of detections,  largely due to the difficulty in observing them.  This study presents the first identification of an enigmatic object, designated ASASSN-19qk,  as an FXRT.  This discovery was made possible by combining data from the Asteroid Small Satellite Survey and ground-based and space-based X-ray telescopes.  Our findings show that ASASSN-19qk is associated with the galaxy IC 2497 and exhibits the typical characteristics of an FXRT, including its unusual behavior and high X-ray emissions.  The X-ray observations of ASASSN-19qk reveal a complex structure consisting of two distinct X-ray sources,  with the primary source exhibiting a hard X-ray spectrum and high X-ray variability.  This discovery has important implications for our understanding of FXRTs and highlights the need for further research and observation of these enigmatic objects.

light in a two-dimensional photonic crystal is made easier when using a two-polarization basis, as it eliminates the need to consider different propagation directions for each polarization. Unfortunately, this level of simplification is not possible with the electric field, due to its perpendicular orientation to the propagation direction. This paper introduces a model that maintains the advantages of the two-polarization approach while using the electric field directly, even in three dimensions. This new model achieves this by approximating the propagation direction of the light with an effective electric field that is parallel to the propagation direction, resulting in a photonic eigenvalue problem that accurately predicts the light's behavior. This approach is made possible by exploiting the relationship between the electric field and the magnetic field in a two-dimensional photonic crystal.

By integrating the quantum Hall barrier concept with a superconducting state, we create the necessary conditions for zero energy modes to emerge.  A wire of 25 micrometers in length and composed of two 50 nanometer thick layers, the application of an axial magnetic field up to 20 Tesla results in the appearance of multiple zero energy peaks.  These peaks are shifted by both the axial and tilting magnetic fields, indicating that the mode's stability is determined by the total momentum of the applied magnetic field. ability of data augmentation is still an open question in machine learning.  This paper investigates the relationship between data augmentation and regularization, specifically, whether the minimum risk achieved with a perturbed input distribution during training is equivalent to that of minimizing expected risk over the training data under maximum a posteriori estimation.  Our analysis shows that the answer depends on the specific data augmentation method employed.  For linear transformations that preserve the origin, such as those found in contrastive learning, our research proves that the perturbed and expected risks are equal.  In contrast, for non-preserving transformations like random cropping, our findings indicate that such methods have regularization effects beyond what maximum a posteriori estimation can explain.  To support our findings, we provide theoretical support via local Hessian analysis and practical data support.

In this study, we examine how a epidemic spreads across a specific type of network, which is made up of interconnected small components. We take a modular approach to model this process, analyzing the different parts of the network separately. We focus on a particular part of the network and simplify its connections to other parts, which we treat as an equivalent, simplified structure.   classification tasks, they often require a large number of labeled training
  images.  To reduce the labeling burden, few-shot learning methods train a
  classifier using a small number of training images, and then adapt it to
  classify new images with even fewer labeled samples.  Current few-shot
  learning approaches primarily focus on square images, but real-world
  applications frequently involve rectangular images with varying aspect
  ratios.  To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for few-shot
  classification of rectangular images, building upon a two-stage task
  adaptation process.  In the first stage, we develop a baseline classifier
  that leverages a multi-head attention mechanism to analyze the aspect ratio
  of query images and incorporates this information into the classification
  process.  In the second stage, we introduce an adaptive meta-learning
  network, which is trained to generate intermediate class embeddings based on
  the aspect ratio of query images and the initial classification
  probabilities.  We evaluate our framework on two benchmark datasets,
  demonstrating its ability to improve upon standard few-shot classification

Specifically, the derivation is performed directly without making use of the generating functional or taking the functional derivative of the electron's renormalization conditions.  Instead, the process is carried out for any Green's function through a clear and explicit formula.  This is achieved by expressing the degree of differentiation of the vacuum expectation value of time-ordered products of electromagnetic currents in terms of the derivative of the Schwinger-Dyson equation.  The formula's coefficients are given by the values of certain position arguments and involve the Wightman functions of the same order.  The correctness of the proposed approach is confirmed by its ability to reproduce the standard results for the two-point function's renormalization, the three-point function, and the four-point function.

In a uniform environment with constant reaction rates, it has been demonstrated that polymers in two-dimensional solutions behave like non-interacting objects after their profile has been rescaled, yet in three-dimensional settings they exist in a unique state determined by the reaction rate.  To investigate the effect of a changing environment, we examine rings of polymers in three dimensions and calculate how average sizes depend on the reaction rate and rescaled ring radius in line with previous studies.  We also explore chains and rings in two dimensions and confirm that their average sizes follow linear laws consistent with theoretical predictions. These findings were confirmed through extensive Monte Carlo simulations and supported by simple numerical path integrals.

characterized by irregular bronchial wall thickness, is a hallmark of emphysema. Computed tomography scans are instrumental in identifying these dilatations, which are typically classified based on their size and shape. Small classifications are less harmful but numerous, whereas large ones are fewer in number but more damaging. Shape-based classifications are easier to identify but require advanced image analysis, while number-based classifications are simpler but demand scanning at high resolutions. This paper introduces the first multi-dimensional bronchial classification system that accounts for both size and shape, leveraging a sophisticated detection algorithm and shape extraction technique. Evaluated on a publicly available dataset, our results demonstrate that this approach can accurately distinguish bronchial types, albeit with room for improvement. Notably, our findings highlight the critical role of three-dimensional connectivity in isolating extensive bronchial structures, outperforming conventional connectivity methods.
